title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated licence-plate recognition system, occurring at the point where a machine-generated alert was handed to a human officer for enforcement. The system matched a plate it had misread to a vehicle reported stolen, and the officer acted on that match in the field. The failure sits at the boundary between detection and decision: the technology produced a candidate identification, and the deployment treated it as sufficient grounds for a armed stop.

The facts describe a system used in a way its own maker says it should not be. Flock stated that alerts require independent verification before enforcement, which indicates the intended workflow includes a human check between the alert and any action. Whether that check was performed, skipped, or impossible in the time available is not established by the reporting. The sheriff's office attributed the misread to an illegal tinted plate cover and characterised the deputy's conduct as reasonable, which places the stated cause on the plate rather than on the system or the officer.

Catching this kind of error requires verification that does not depend on the same automated match being correct, such as a visual comparison of the plate against the stolen-vehicle record before a stop is initiated. The reporting does not establish what verification, if any, occurred, nor does it establish that the plate cover caused the misread as a matter of fact rather than as the department's account. A misread is a technical outcome, and the attribution of it to an illegal cover remains an assertion by one party.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, 42, of York County, South Carolina, was detained at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction and called the deputy’s actions “reasonable.” Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
